forecaster.notes: Plan mode was on, so I edited no files and used only read-only web research. The Senate distribution starts from the 2026-11-04 count (Peltola +637 on first choices). I added FairVote's estimates of where Heikes and Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. ballots go next (Heikes about 44% to Dan S. Sullivan and 16% to Peltola; Jr. about 33% to Peltola and 22% to Dan S. Sullivan). That nets Dan S. Sullivan roughly 950 votes, which would make the counted ballots about 49.9% Peltola after tabulation. Roughly 47,000 early and absentee ballots in hand, plus late mail, questioned and overseas ballots, are expected to lean Peltola. Her campaign says she took about 56.6% of early and mail ballots counted so far, and a NYT analysis expects her lead to grow. AP has Democrats at 54 Senate seats with Alaska and Mississippi uncalled, so Senate control does not depend on Alaska.

research_summary: Unofficial count as of 11/4: Peltola 102,962 (48.18%), Dan S. Sullivan 102,325 (47.88%), Heikes 4,846 and Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. 3,600, with about 74% counted. Campaigns put about 20,000 early and 27,000 absentee ballots in hand, plus late and overseas ballots. A Sullivan campaign memo says he needs about 49.5% of the two-candidate vote among remaining ballots. Peltola's campaign says she won about 56.6% of early and mail ballots counted so far. A NYT analysis expects Peltola's lead to grow and finds she was the next choice of most Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. voters. FairVote's estimate from the incomplete cast-vote record has Heikes ballots moving mostly to Dan S. Sullivan and Jr. ballots leaning to Peltola. Final polling averages had Peltola ahead by about 2 points. Governor: Kreiss-Tomkins 49.1% of first choices; FairVote's preliminary tabulation puts him ahead of Wilson about 55-45. Ballot Measure 2: Yes 48.15% and trailing. Courts: DOJ's suit was dismissed for lack of standing on 11/1 and is on appeal to the Ninth Circuit, which is unlikely to rule before certification. Peltola's campaign is suing for absentee-ballot records. Nationally, AP has Democrats at 54 seats and Republicans at 44, with Mississippi (Colom leading by about 2,574 at 97% counted) and Alaska uncalled. Economy: BLS has Alaska's seasonally adjusted unemployment at 4.3% for September 2026 (preliminary). EIA puts Alaska crude output at 427 kb/d for August 2026, and Pikka is ramping toward 80 kb/d.

dem_share.reasoning: After tabulation, the ballots counted so far come to about 49.9% Peltola. Outstanding ballots, probably about 60,000 to 75,000, lean Peltola: about 53-56% of the two-candidate vote, judging from counted early and mail ballots and the pattern in 2022 and 2024, when Peltola gained in late counts. That puts my median final share near 50.75%. Sullivan still wins if the late ballots split roughly evenly or the next-choice transfers favor him more than estimated.

bm2_yes_share.reasoning: Yes stands at 48.15% with about 74% counted. In 2024 the late count moved the repeal measure slightly toward No. Yes moves opposite to Peltola's share because the same late, Democratic-leaning ballots drive both. Where Peltola does better, Yes falls by roughly 0.3 points per Senate range.

gov_dem_share.reasoning: Kreiss-Tomkins has 49.1% of first choices. Most Bronson and Taylor ballots (about 46,000 votes) should move to Wilson, which gives roughly 53-55% for Kreiss-Tomkins in the final round; FairVote's preliminary tabulation has 55-45. His share rises with Peltola's because late ballots lean the same way in both races.

recount.reasoning: Under AS 15.20.430 a losing candidate or 10 voters can apply for a recount, and the state pays when the margin is within about 0.5% of votes cast. Within half a point the loser almost surely asks for one, and an aggressive Republican push after a narrow Peltola win (Trump has claimed Sullivan won, and DOJ is litigating) makes a recount more likely there. Senate control does not depend on Alaska, which lowers the stakes somewhat.

contest.reasoning: Alaska election contests are rare but do follow close, disputed races. If Peltola wins, the 'decoy Dan' confusion argument offers Republicans or allied voters a ready claim, especially when the margin is close to the Jr. vote of about 3,600. If Sullivan wins narrowly, the Peltola side could contest over rejected absentee ballots.

court_order.reasoning: Courts rarely bar or delay certification. The district court found DOJ lacked standing, and a Ninth Circuit stay before certification looks unlikely. Alaska courts handle disputes after certification through recounts and contests. The risk is highest when Peltola wins narrowly, the case DOJ's suit targets.

winner_sworn.reasoning: Alaska normally certifies in late November, and even in 2010, with a recount and contest, Murkowski was certified on December 30 and seated in January. A Democratic-majority Senate would promptly seat a certified Peltola and would almost certainly seat a certified Sullivan. The risk comes from a long recount or contest pushing past January 31 in the closest ranges.

peltola_senator.reasoning: This tracks winner_sworn in the ranges where Peltola wins. In the ranges where Sullivan wins it is near zero, apart from a small chance in the closest range that a contest or Senate dispute reverses the result.

dem_caucus.reasoning: AP has Democrats at 54 seats, with Alaska and Mississippi uncalled. I give Colom about a 0.8 chance of holding his roughly 2,500-vote lead in Mississippi, which has no recount. The total is 54, plus Peltola if she is seated, plus Colom. I leave a small allowance for vacancies or party switches.

sullivan_post.reasoning: Defeated senators from the president's party sometimes get appointments; Loeffler and Perdue did, but years later. Within seven months it is less likely, especially with a Democratic Senate after January 3. Sullivan is a Marine reservist with Trump's backing, and Pentagon, State or ambassador roles are plausible. A drawn-out contest after a narrow loss could delay any move.

baseline.source: BLS Local Area Unemployment Statistics, https://www.bls.gov/web/laus/laumstrk.htm

ak_unemployment.reasoning: The seasonally adjusted state rate moves slowly; the typical three-month change is 0.1-0.3 points, and annual revisions add noise. It was 4.3% in September 2026, down from 4.7% a year earlier. The Senate result does not plausibly affect December's rate, so the forecast is the same in every range.

baseline.source: EIA Petroleum Supply Monthly, series MCRFPAK2, https://www.eia.gov/dnav/pet/hist/LeafHandler.ashx?n=PET&s=MCRFPAK2&f=M

ak_oil.reasoning: EIA had 427 kb/d for August 2026 and 428 for January 2026. Winter output usually runs about 5-15 kb/d above August. Pikka was producing about 23 kb/d in August, aiming for an 80 kb/d plateau, and could add another 20-50 kb/d by January. Legacy fields decline a few percent a year. That gives a median near 460 kb/d, with downside risk if Pikka ramps slowly or a facility goes down. Production in January 2027 does not depend on the Senate result.
